name: Outdoor Entertainment

seo.title: Outdoor Entertainment | DAVG
seo.description: A dining terrace, garden, and pool are different zones. Speaker placement, sun, weather, and cable routes shape the outdoor system.

hero.heading: Put the sound near the people. Match the screen to the exposure.
hero.deck: A dining terrace, garden, and pool are different zones. Speaker placement, sun, weather, and cable routes shape the outdoor system.

study: A derived outdoor plan and a neutral installation section. Speaker photographs are Episode, not Sonance.

chapters.title: Where will people actually spend time?
paragraphs: A table needs comfortable sound around seated conversation. A garden may need several listening pockets; a pool introduces distance, hard surfaces and different activity.
Map those areas before choosing speakers. Independent zones let a quiet dinner and a more active gathering use different sources or levels where the system supports it.
Include nearby property boundaries in the design. Distributed sound can reduce the need to turn up one distant speaker, but it does not eliminate sound beyond the listening area.
chapters.visual: Illustrative landscape plan with listening areas, seats and boundaries. Show no fabricated sound-pressure contours.

chapters.title: Landscape and surface speakers solve different placement problems.
paragraphs: Surface-mounted speakers can serve a terrace from the building. Landscape speakers can place sound closer to seating and paths without relying on a wall.
Subwoofers handle lower frequencies and need their own placement and installation detail. A buried design still has specified exposure, drainage and access requirements.
Select the speaker family, amplification and wiring method together. Sonance Landscape and Garden systems have different configurations; neither is a universal recipe for every property.
chapters.visual: Actual surface speaker, landscape satellite and subwoofer, each before and after installation. Caption exact model and installation requirements.

chapters.title: Covered does not always mean protected.
paragraphs: An indoor television under a roof still encounters outdoor temperature, humidity and wind-driven conditions. The selected outdoor display needs to suit its actual exposure.
Full-sun and partial-sun models have different installation guidance. Check the exact model against the screen’s orientation and the hours people will watch.
Brightness alone does not remove reflections or make a poor viewing position comfortable. Review glare, mounting, cable access and the manufacturer’s environmental limits together.
chapters.visual: Actual outdoor TV installation at expected viewing times; annotate roof coverage and sun direction. Exact-model product view alongside.

chapters.title: The buried work decides how clean the finished space looks.
paragraphs: Cable routes must fit the landscape, equipment and installation method. Planting, irrigation, drainage and future digging all affect where those routes should go.
A new terrace offers an opportunity to plan conduit and service points before hardscape is placed. An existing patio may require a different route or a smaller initial scope.
Coordinate with the landscape and electrical teams. Exterior lighting circuits, display power and network equipment have different requirements from speaker cable.
chapters.visual: Real route, conduit/service point and finished landscape details. No generic burial-depth rules.

chapters.title: The patio should have its own controls.
paragraphs: A patio scene can select music in the intended zone and adjust supported exterior lighting. A viewing scene can select the TV source and its sound path.
Wireless control needs coverage where people sit. The network route to an outdoor display or controller matters just as much as the speaker placement.
Set zone names and volume limits the household understands. Use a quiet-hours routine if requested, without promising that an automated setting can prevent every disturbance.
chapters.visual: Dining and Viewing states of the same terrace with a real interface and short action list.

chapters.title: Commission it outside.
paragraphs: Listen from the seats, walk the paths and check the property edges. Confirm the sound balance and controls at normal use levels rather than only beside the equipment.
Check the display at the intended viewing time. Document environmental limits, shutdown or storage instructions, and maintenance for the selected equipment.
Colorado weather makes model-specific temperature and installation limits part of the selection. A weather rating is not permission to ignore the manufacturer’s instructions.
chapters.visual: Genuine daytime/sunset viewing and listening checks. Maintenance schedule names the selected products.

projectPaths.title: Improve the existing patio
projectPaths.body: Survey seating, exposure, power and cable paths. Begin with the zones that can be served cleanly without reopening the whole landscape.

projectPaths.title: Coordinate with the outdoor work
projectPaths.body: Plan speaker routes, display location, service points and network coverage before hardscape and planting are finished.

projectPaths.title: Design the property as connected zones
projectPaths.body: Work with architecture and landscape teams on listening areas, sun, equipment locations and interior/exterior connections. Keep future service access in the plan.

scopeOptions.label: Good — a defined outdoor area
scopeOptions.scope: One listening or viewing zone, exposure-appropriate equipment, practical routing and installed checks.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Power, network and hardscape work are itemized.

scopeOptions.label: Better — multiple outdoor zones
scopeOptions.scope: Dining/garden or pool areas with suitable speaker distribution, source control and planned display exposure.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Zone boundaries, amplification and routes follow the property.

scopeOptions.label: Best — coordinated landscape system
scopeOptions.scope: Early landscape design, distributed sound, planned viewing, lighting integration and documented seasonal care.
scopeOptions.dependencies: More coverage does not mean louder operation; every added zone needs a defined use.

faqs.question: Can I put an indoor TV under the patio roof?
faqs.answer: A roof does not remove all outdoor exposure. Select equipment against actual temperature, moisture, sunlight and manufacturer installation limits.

faqs.question: Will landscape speakers disturb neighbors?
faqs.answer: They can. Placement closer to listeners may reduce required level, but sound still travels; we review boundaries and normal listening levels.

faqs.question: Can the patio use the indoor music system?
faqs.answer: When the sources, amplification, controls and network design support that zone. Outdoor equipment still needs its own suitable installation.

faqs.question: What changes cost?
faqs.answer: Zones, speaker/subwoofer choices, display exposure, power/network work, trenching, hardscape access and landscape coordination.

inquiry.heading: Start with the project you have.
inquiry.body: Tell us which rooms matter, what already exists, and when construction starts. Share plans or photographs if you have them.

openingQA.question: How do you make outdoor sound and viewing comfortable?
answer: Place suitable speakers near the listening areas, and select the display against its actual sun and weather exposure. Then coordinate power, network and cable routes with the landscape.
That gives each outdoor area a defined role. It does not require one loud speaker or the same equipment across the entire property.
